## [2026-10-23](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-23.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Memory-Aware Reward Modeling: Learning Human Preferences for LLM Memory Use](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31272>)

This study asks whether personal memories actually make an assistant’s answers more useful to the person who supplied them, combining user judgments with an interpretable rubric-based preference model. On 291 strong-preference pairs, participant-held-out evaluation reaches 72.8% prediction accuracy versus a 55.0% majority baseline, giving developers a way to evaluate appropriate memory use beyond factual recall.

**Published:** 2026-10-22 · **First seen:** 2026-10-23T10:04:57.196Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Memory Evaluation, Human Preferences, Personalization, Rubric Models

**Public availability:** 2026-10-23T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/new>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.31272v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 3–6 and Appendices A–F report 821 quality-filtered judgments from 87 participants, comparing responses generated with and without nine retrieved personal-memory entries. Candidate pairs were screened for substantial memory-grounded differences before annotation. Under ordinary prompting, memory/no-memory/tie preferences are 38.7%/41.9%/19.4%; direction differs by response generator. The learned model uses rubric features and L2 logistic regression on the 291 clear “much better” pairs. Rubric induction, standardization and nested regularization selection use training participants only; five participant-separated folds are repeated across ten shuffles, with predictions averaged before accuracy. Table 3 reports 72.8% overall accuracy against a 55.0% majority baseline; response-only features achieve 67.0%. Receipt 2026-10-22T13:43:33Z is preserved; original cs.CL October 23 new-submission listing plus the official schedule supports inferred 2026-10-23T00:00Z availability. No earlier matching author release was established.

**Limitations:** This is a small, screened offline preference study, not representative evidence for all assistant queries or a trained memory-management policy. Only 291 strong-preference pairs enter the learned-model evaluation; aggregate prompting differences are descriptive and vary by generator. Length and heading features are influential, so gains cannot be attributed solely to memory-specific judgment. It does not measure longitudinal agent behavior or downstream RL improvements. Some baseline-label wording and collection-prompt counts differ between main text and appendices; claims here use the stable table values and avoid the disputed labels/counts. No public author code or dataset artifact was verified.

### [LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale](<https://www.anthropic.com/research/formal-verification>)

Anthropic and Theorem use Claude to turn existing fuzz-test entry points into specifications for compiled programs, then generate proofs that Rocq checks against modeled execution semantics. This makes proof-producing coding agents a concrete software-hardening workflow, while the guarantees remain conditional on the particular binaries, specifications and trusted models.

**Evidence:** engineering-report; full-text. The complete blog and six-page appendix describe the workflow and report proofs for 239 entry points across 123 libraries, with an input bound of 64 MiB; the inspected public release contains proofs for 60 entry points in 25 libraries. This is a new dated research disclosure with inspectable proof artifacts; no proof checker was executed here.

**Limitations:** The public statements concern fixed-budget, static RISC-V/Linux binaries and reachable harness behavior, rather than whole-library correctness or deployed x86/ARM systems. The released agreement proofs do not establish termination. Patches regenerate specifications, creating a potential shortcut that the authors report auditing; semantics, theorem statements, checker and tooling remain trusted. ### [MultiLangBench and behavior-preserving COBOL migration evaluation](<https://openai.com/index/low-resource-programming-languages/>)

OpenAI introduced MultiLangBench, which tests whether coding models can implement a SQLite-compatible engine across 20 programming languages, alongside a separate COBOL migration evaluation requiring exact output preservation. The released tests give developers a concrete way to assess long coding sessions in less common languages, while the authors report substantial accuracy gains for their latest models under these specific settings. The migration suite remains hidden, and success on either evaluation does not establish production readiness or general superiority across software engineering tasks.

Model and reasoning-effort comparisons do not isolate a training recipe or architecture change, and estimated API cost depends on output usage and pricing. ### [MS-Eval: Benchmarking Sub-Agent Delegation and Orchestration in MCP-Intensive Working Scenarios](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22869>)

MS-Eval pairs 166 tool-intensive work tasks with annotated delegation plans and a controlled harness, evaluating when subagents help as well as their success, critical-path steps and API-token cost. Its eight-model study shows that specialization and context offloading can help, while unnecessary delegation often adds cost; this gives agent builders a more informative comparison than assuming that adding subagents improves every model.

Tasks span eight Toolathlon-Gym scenarios, with 89 annotated as delegation-needed and 77 not-needed; four delegation variants share a Kimi-Code scaffold. A 166-task comparison evaluates eight models, while the variant comparison uses DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731. Specialized roles score MSQ 20.8 versus 11.6 for general roles and 17.6 for plan-first in that setup. Critical steps count each parallel wave by its slowest subagent, not measured wall time; API billing is a fixed-price estimate. **Limitations:** One simulated tool environment and one harness; role prompts change the main agent even when it delegates nothing, and 305 of 625 categorized beneficial cases are main-agent-only. Delegation priors reflect the authors' parallelism/context-offloading assumptions; matching uses an LLM tagger and the custom MSQ weighting is not a universal quality score. Resource utilities condition on selected/successful subsets, and efficiency is critical steps rather than latency. No author implementation or independent reproduction verified.

### [GraphACM: Graph-based Action Consistency Measurement for Uncertainty Quantification in LLM Agents](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22031>)

GraphACM aligns repeated agent runs into a shared state-action graph and measures whether they choose the same actions in comparable decision contexts. This training-free signal localizes behavioral disagreement and distinguishes more reliably solved tasks in the tested environments, helping builders assess execution stability without treating consistency as a correctness guarantee.

### [On the estimation and validity of AI time horizons—a statistical look at the METR plot](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12466>)

This statistical audit re-estimates METR's software-task time horizons with shared monotone splines and item-response models, testing predictions by holding out entire task families. It finds that equal multipliers in human task duration can represent different capability gains, providing diagnostics for interpreting agent progress without treating a single horizon number as a universal capability scale.

## [2026-10-07](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-07.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Agent in a Bottle: Can LLM Agents Turn Their Capabilities Into Cheap, Scalable Artifacts?](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08775>)

BOTTLED tests whether an agent can build and apply a reusable program or smaller model to an entire unlabeled workload under fixed time and API budgets. It measures the practical ability to turn expensive per-example competence into an economical batch solution, revealing failures that ordinary zero-shot accuracy misses.

**Published:** 2026-10-06 · **First seen:** 2026-10-07T10:05:04Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Agent Evaluation, Reusable Artifacts, Amortized Cost

**Public availability:** 2026-10-07T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.AI/recent>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.08775v1>) · [Code](<https://github.com/aktsonthalia/bottled>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Across ten models, three tasks and two runs per setting, 31 of 60 agent runs underperform the stronger of two small-model distillation baselines with the same weighted-token budget. A populated public repository provides the harness, budget enforcement, datasets scripts and baselines.

**Limitations:** Only three narrow NLP workloads and one harness are evaluated. Zero-shot scores and full-workload costs are estimated from 1,000 examples, while bottled predictions cover the full workload. Equal token budgets do not mean identical monetary or compute budgets, and contamination checking uses an agentic judge.
